suggestions.rationale: Sexual dysfunction is a recognized long-term outcome after cauda equina syndrome, and systematic-review evidence identifies erectile dysfunction as the most frequently reported male sexual disorder in studied CES populations. This supports a clinically relevant CES/erectile-dysfunction relationship for research when erectile dysfunction is documented after established CES with compatible sacral neurologic involvement, but population-level outcome data do not by themselves establish an individual causal nexus and do not exclude vascular, endocrine, medication-related, psychogenic, or other contributors.
evidenceGaps: Clinical documentation confirming erectile dysfunction and its onset, persistence, and severity
Records establishing the cauda equina syndrome diagnosis, neurologic level and severity, and relevant sacral findings such as bladder, bowel, perianal sensory, or other sacral nerve-root dysfunction
Pre-CES sexual-function history and chronology comparing CES onset or decompression with erectile-dysfunction onset or worsening
Evaluation of competing erectile-dysfunction contributors, including vascular disease, diabetes, endocrine disorders, medications, psychiatric factors, and other neurologic disease

Urology, neurology, spine, or other qualified medical opinion addressing whether the individual erectile dysfunction is medically attributable to or aggravated by the documented CES rather than an alternative cause

sourceReferences.citation: Moradi et al., BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders (2025), PMID 40380123
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review of sexual dysfunction after lumbar disc herniation and cauda equina syndrome reported persistent sexual problems after CES and identified erectile dysfunction as the most prevalent male sexual disorder; supports a condition-specific clinical relationship, not automatic individual causation.

sourceReferences.citation: Najjar et al., European Spine Journal (2026), PMID 42472710
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review of long-term CES outcomes found sexual dysfunction common and persistent, with a pooled estimate of 58.4% and limited evidence linking worse outcomes to markers of sacral nerve-root involvement; supports long-term clinical relevance while preserving uncertainty about individual causation and baseline function.
